topStory.headline: NPR: 85% of Undergraduates Use A.I. for Coursework as Policies Diverge
topStory.summary:
More than three years after ChatGPT debuted, about 85% of undergraduates use A.I. for coursework including brainstorming ideas, outlining papers, and studying for exams, according to a survey by Inside Higher Ed and Generation Lab cited by NPR. Roughly 19% also reported using A.I. to write full essays.

Faculty approaches vary widely. At Johnson County Community College in Kansas City, English professor Dan Cryer opposes A.I. in writing assignments, describing generative A.I. for essays as "bringing a forklift to the gym." At Johnson C. Smith University, professor Leslie Clement encourages responsible A.I. use in her classes, allowing students to use it for outlines, feedback, and comparing sources. She co-created a course called "African Diaspora and A.I." examining how these tools affect people of African descent globally.

Students report mixed feelings about A.I. use. At the University of Minnesota, senior Aysa Tarana stopped using ChatGPT because it felt like "outsourcing my thinking." At UNC Chapel Hill, student Hannah Elder refuses A.I.-generated content, viewing her writing as "like a fingerprint to the world." More than half of students who use A.I. for coursework acknowledge it can make them think less deeply.

stories.headline: UK Survey: 95% of University Students Use A.I., 15% for Companionship
stories.summary: The Higher Education Policy Institute surveyed 1,054 UK undergraduates and found 95% use A.I. in at least one way, with 94% using it to support assessed work, according to HEPI. Notably, 12% directly include A.I.-generated text in assignments, up from 3% in 2024, and 15% report using A.I. for companionship or addressing loneliness.

stories.headline: Writing Faculty Pass Resolution Affirming Right to Refuse A.I.
stories.summary: The Conference on College Composition and Communication passed a resolution affirming that students and faculty may opt out of using generative A.I. in writing instruction without penalty, according to Inside Higher Ed. The resolution cites concerns about data privacy, academic freedom, and erosion of critical thinking through writing practice.

stories.headline: Johnson C. Smith Professor Creates 'African Diaspora and A.I.' Course
stories.summary: Professor Leslie Clement at Johnson C. Smith University encourages responsible A.I. use while teaching students to critically examine its global impacts, according to NPR. Her course explores how A.I. affects people of African descent, including cobalt mining for hardware, labor conditions, and contributions of Black researchers to the field.

stories.headline: College Board: 74% of Faculty See Students Using A.I. for Essays
stories.summary: A survey of over 3,000 faculty found that 74% report students using A.I. for essay writing, with only 21% feeling confident guiding A.I. use, according to the College Board. Faculty at selective institutions report higher concern, while faculty at open enrollment colleges view A.I. more as a practical instructional tool.
